unit.title: Subjunctive in Relative & Concessive Clauses
unit.subtitle: Unknown antecedents and 'no matter how much' with the subjunctive

grammar.title: When the thing you're describing might not exist
grammar.intro: In a relative clause (a clause that describes a noun), the mood depends on one thing: is the noun real and known, or unknown, hypothetical, or nonexistent? If you know it exists, use the indicative. If you're searching for it, doubt it, or deny it, use the subjunctive. The same instinct powers concessive clauses — por más que, por mucho que, and aunque — where you concede a point that may or may not hold.

sections.heading: Known vs. unknown antecedent
sections.body: Compare the two. If the person or thing is specific and real, the verb stays indicative. If it's hypothetical — someone you're looking for but haven't found — switch to the subjunctive:

ex.en: I know someone who speaks English.
I'm looking for someone who speaks English.

sections.heading: Nonexistent antecedent: no hay nadie que…
sections.body: When you deny that the thing exists at all — no hay nadie que, no hay nada que — the subjunctive is obligatory. The same goes for describing something you need but don't yet have:

ex.es: No hay nadie que sepa la respuesta.
ex.en: There's no one who knows the answer.
I need a book that's easy.

sections.heading: Concession: por más/mucho que + subjunctive
sections.body: To say no matter how much, use por más que or por mucho que + subjunctive. And aunque takes the subjunctive when you concede a hypothetical (even if it were / even if it turns out to be):
conj: no matter how much I study
no matter how hard you try

ex.en: No matter how much I study, I don't pass.
Even if it rains, I'll go running.

takeaways: Known/real antecedent → indicative: Conozco a alguien que habla inglés.
Unknown/sought antecedent → subjunctive: Busco a alguien que hable inglés.
Nonexistent → subjunctive: No hay nadie que sepa; Necesito un libro que sea fácil.
Concession: por más/mucho que + subjunctive; aunque + subjunctive for a hypothetical.

mistakes.w: Busco a alguien que habla francés.
mistakes.r: Busco a alguien que hable francés.
mistakes.why: The person is unknown (you're still looking), so the relative clause needs the subjunctive: hable.

mistakes.w: No hay nadie que sabe la verdad.
mistakes.r: No hay nadie que sepa la verdad.
mistakes.why: A nonexistent antecedent (no hay nadie) forces the subjunctive: sepa.

mistakes.w: Por mucho que estudio, no apruebo.
mistakes.r: Por mucho que estudie, no apruebo.
mistakes.why: Por mucho que expresses a concession and takes the subjunctive: estudie.

exercises.prompt_en: I'm looking for someone who speaks English.
exercises.no: You're looking for an unknown person, so use the subjunctive: “hable”.

exercises.prompt_en: I know someone who speaks English.
exercises.no: The person is real and known, so use the indicative: “habla”.

exercises.prompt: Build: “There's no one who knows the answer.”
exercises.no: “No hay nadie que sepa la respuesta” — a nonexistent antecedent needs the subjunctive.

exercises.prompt: Por mucho que ___, no apruebo. (estudiar, yo)
exercises.prompt_en: No matter how much I study, I don't pass.
exercises.hint: Concession — 'por mucho que' takes the subjunctive.
exercises.no: Por mucho que triggers the subjunctive: “estudie”.

exercises.prompt: Match each Spanish clause to its meaning.

exercises.tts: Necesito un libro que sea fácil.
accepted: necesito un libro que sea facil
exercises.translation: I need a book that's easy.
exercises.no: It was: “Necesito un libro que sea fácil.” (I need a book that's easy.)

lines.es: Necesitamos a alguien para el proyecto. ¿Alguna idea?
lines.en: We need someone for the project. Any ideas?

options.text: Busco a alguien que sepa alemán.
Busco a alguien que sabe alemán.
Busco a alguien que sabrá alemán.

exercises.no: The person is still unknown, so use the subjunctive: “que sepa alemán”.

exercises.en: There's no one who knows the answer.
